prize_parts.citation: for the prediction of flat electronic bands at the magic twist angle in bilayer graphene and the experimental discovery of correlated insulating and superconducting states in twisted bilayer graphene

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene as a single part. I have tightened the citation after hearing Eriksson and Lindroth, so that it names only the flat-band prediction and the observed correlated insulating and superconducting states, not the pairing mechanism. The achievement is a prediction followed by a decisive experiment, and the experiment was reproduced within a short time by independent groups using transport, scanning tunnelling and local-probe spectroscopy. That reproduction, which I can judge as an experimentalist, tells me the phenomenology is robust even while the interpretation is open. Twist angle is a continuous, controllable parameter, and the field of moire materials it started has changed what can be built and measured. The round-1 exchange showed me that the real contest is between this and the optical lattice clock, and that the contest is about what the prize rewards, not about the quality of either.
statement.case_against: Maturity is the strongest objection and the first round did not remove it. The experiments date from 2018, the superconducting mechanism is unsettled, and a prize now could precede the interpretation. Lindroth's point that the clock has a decade-long record of independent confirmation that graphene lacks is correct. Attribution is also imperfect: Lopes dos Santos, Peres and Castro Neto preceded the 2011 continuum model, and Cao, Fatemi and the Dean group did experimental work that a three-name cap cannot credit. By contrast, the optical lattice clock has a cleaner two-name attribution and more settled confirmation, and I find that case harder to dismiss after reading Kroll's argument that the magic-wavelength condition is a concept and not only an engineering refinement.

responses.point: Kroll argues that the magic-wavelength condition is a concept, because it removes the trade-off between trapping atoms and perturbing the clock transition, and that the claim rests on an instrument-enabled change in what can be measured.
responses.response: This moved me. I had treated the clock mainly as a refinement of the programmes honoured in 2005 and 2012, and your point that the magic-wavelength condition solves a different problem from the comb or single-ion control is fair. I still do not see what new physics the clock has taught us so far: no deviation from existing theory has been found, and the redefinition of the second has not happened. Your own words, that the claim rests on measurement impact, are why I keep it as my first alternative and not as my preferred part. I would accept it without objection if the committee turns that way.

responses.point: Lindroth regards twisted bilayer graphene as the natural next candidate but not the one to prefer this year, because the pairing mechanism is debated and the clock has a longer record of independent confirmation. She asks that any graphene credit address the earlier Lopes dos Santos, Peres and Castro Neto theory.
responses.response: I accept the maturity gap and have not removed it; I can only argue that a citation limited to flat bands and correlated phases does not need the mechanism to be settled, as the phenomenology has been reproduced widely. On Lopes dos Santos, Peres and Castro Neto, I propose that the citation says the prediction of flat bands at a magic angle, which is specifically the Bistritzer-MacDonald calculation, and not the first suggestion that twist changes the band structure. That is defensible, but I agree it cannot be called airtight, and I would not claim it is.

responses.point: Mehlig says the 2016 topological-phases prize did not recognise time-reversal-invariant topological insulators or quantum spin Hall edge states, and that twisted graphene is only eight years old, so he would wait.
responses.response: Your reply answers my 2016 caveat on B008: the Z2 classification and the HgTe edge transport are a separate principle, and I now regard the overlap as less of an obstacle. That is why B008 stays on my list of alternatives. Our disagreement on graphene is one of timing, and I would not call it settled. I do think that waiting for the superconducting mechanism sets a higher bar than we apply to a prize for an observed effect. Several earlier prizes honoured discoveries whose microscopic explanation remained open when they were awarded.

responses.point: Pearce pairs the optical lattice clock with IceCube credited to Halzen alone, to keep the union at three people, and concedes that a lone name for a collaboration of hundreds is the weak point.
responses.response: I accept that the diffuse flux is a real discovery and that the objection is about credit. A single-name credit does answer the attribution problem I raised in round 1, but it creates a different one: the result is a collaboration's, and the detector construction and analysis rest on Karle and the wider team as much as on Halzen. As a microscopist I would be wary of any citation that assigns an instrument-driven discovery to one person. I also still cannot judge the statistics of the source associations, and your point that they remain at moderate significance does not help me. I would therefore not support the second part, and I think a single coherent achievement is better than pairing unrelated fields.

uncertainties: Whether the unresolved origin of superconductivity in magic-angle graphene makes a prize premature, or whether the established, widely reproduced phenomenology suffices.
Whether the clock counts as a discovery in the sense of the Nobel criteria, and whether the pending redefinition of the second should delay it.
How the prize would handle Cao, Fatemi and the Dean group under a three-name cap, and the earlier Lopes dos Santos, Peres and Castro Neto theory.
How robust the IceCube source associations are beyond the diffuse flux, which I cannot evaluate from my own field.
statement.conflict_note: No direct conflict with the credited names of B029. For B043 I repeat the possible connection I flagged in round 1: my long-running academic exchanges with Japanese universities and my University of Tokyo fellowship are relevant to Katori, with no documented collaboration, and I would not treat it as disqualifying. Goran Johansson is a Chalmers colleague, but no shortlisted ballot credits a Chalmers person, and I have no other conflict to add.
